solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Judge had robe altered

indicators.note: altered says the letters of 'had robe' are changed round into a new order

explanation.surface: A judge's gown has been taken in by the tailor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Judge' looks like a job title, but it means the Old Testament judge of Israel; 'altered' rearranges HADROBE.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Book of Judges, Deborah was a prophetess who served as one of the judges of Israel.

clue.text: Silly poets' egos may be seen in peculiar gait

indicators.note: silly signals that the letters of the poets and their egos are muddled up

explanation.surface: Vain poets strut about in an odd fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silly' rearranges POETSEGOS.
explanation.definitionFit: The stiff-legged military march is a famously odd way of walking.

clue.text: Religious writings in brown with upsetting pictures?

parts.note: tan is a light brown colour

indicators.note: in a down clue, upsetting turns a word upside down, so it reads from the bottom up

parts.note: pictures, paintings and drawings are art

explanation.surface: Sacred texts in brown covers containing disturbing illustrations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upsetting' turns ART to TRA. 'pictures?' seems to describe the writings, but it is just ART.
explanation.definitionFit: The tantras are Hindu and Buddhist scriptures dealing with ritual and meditation.

clue.text: Most quiet end to this match — it's bad getting caught

indicators.note: the end to a word is its final letter, here taken from 'this'
getting caught says the 'bad' word is held inside the 'match' word

parts.note: a Test is an international cricket match
ill means bad, as in ill effects

explanation.surface: Commentary on the dull closing stages of a cricket match marred by a catch.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a cricket Test where a batsman is caught; 'getting caught' is really the container signal, holding the bad piece inside the match.
explanation.definitionFit: Superlative of still, meaning calm and silent, so the most quiet.

clue.text: When agitated, he got spiteful, no mistake!

indicators.note: agitated says the letters of the fodder are stirred about into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A man gets nasty when riled and insists he has not made an error.
explanation.walkthrough: 'agitated' rearranges HEGOTSPITEFUL with NO; 'no' looks like part of 'no mistake!' but is fodder, and 'mistake' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A verbal blunder, an accidental wrong word blurted out, is an idiomatic error of speech.

clue.text: One way of saying artist entered to reveal secret

parts.note: entered means came in, said here in the inverted form 'in came'
RA is a Royal Academician, a crossword artist

explanation.surface: A painter walked in and spilt a confidence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One way of saying artist entered' means phrasing it as 'in came RA'; those words run together give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal phrase for proceedings held in private, away from the public, hence done confidentially.

clue.text: Type of delivery adjacent to reception area

parts.note: a lob is a high, looping ball delivered in cricket or tennis
by means beside, next to

explanation.surface: A parcel delivery is left next to the front desk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'delivery' suggests the post, but here it is a ball bowled or hit.
explanation.definitionFit: An entrance hall of a hotel or theatre where visitors are received.

clue.text: Sort of problem not in the foreground

definitions.meaning: a hitch or reverse that delays progress
placed further away, positioned to the rear, read as two words

explanation.definitionFit: As one word it is a reverse or hitch; as two words it means placed back from the front.

clue.text: A refusal by cleric to go round Italian city

indicators.note: to go round says the whole string of pieces is turned about and read backwards

parts.note: no is a refusal
Rev is short for Reverend, a cleric

explanation.surface: A priest turns down the chance of a tour of an Italian city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to go round' turns ANOREV back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: Verona is a city in the Veneto in northern Italy, setting of Romeo and Juliet.

clue.text: Brood at home — one of the youngsters took food

parts.note: in means at home
a cub is a young fox, bear or lion, or a junior Scout
ate means took food

explanation.surface: A parent sulks at home while a child has a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brood' looks like sulking, but it is the verb for sitting on eggs.
explanation.definitionFit: To brood eggs is to sit on them and keep them warm until they hatch.

clue.text: Roof needs seemingly 45 minutes group work

parts.note: 45 minutes is three-quarters of an hour, so three of the four letters of that word
a set is a group
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: Roof repair needs a team working for three-quarters of an hour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seemingly 45 minutes' is a visual joke: three quarters of the word for sixty minutes, HOU.
explanation.definitionFit: The top of a building, its roof or ridge, a dated compound word.

clue.text: Constructed a spoken message requesting assistance

indicators.note: spoken says the words are to be heard said aloud rather than read

parts.note: constructed means made, followed by the article

explanation.surface: Someone put together a radio call for help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made a', said quickly, sounds like the distress call.
explanation.definitionFit: Mayday is the international radio distress signal, from the French m'aidez.

clue.text: Sir John is given a flower by workforce

parts.note: a flower is something that flows, a river; the Fal is a river in Cornwall
staff are a workforce

explanation.surface: A knight receives a bouquet from his employees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flower' is a crossword river (something that flows); the Fal runs through Cornwall in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir John Falstaff is Shakespeare's fat, roguish knight in the Henry IV plays.

clue.text: A traditional way to get the traveller's money?

definitions.text: A traditional way to get the traveller's money?

parts.words: A traditional way to get the traveller's money?
parts.note: an old road with a gate where each passer-by paid a toll; it also hints at a highwayman's robbery

explanation.walkthrough: 'way' is a road, and the 'money' taken is a toll, not a robbery.
explanation.definitionFit: An old toll road, gated so travellers had to pay before passing.

clue.text: Lacking purpose and unable to score

definitions.meaning: with no points on the board

explanation.definitionFit: It means futile, and literally having no points, as a team that fails to score.

clue.text: Hint of fog and competitor losing heart? It makes for a bad test!

parts.note: a mist is a faint, light fog

indicators.note: losing heart says the central letter of the word for competitor is dropped

parts.note: a rival is a competitor

explanation.surface: Faint fog and a disheartened competitor make for a poor examination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing heart' takes the middle V from RIVAL to leave RIAL; 'test' is a trial in court, not an exam.
explanation.definitionFit: A trial ended without a valid verdict through error, a failed hearing in court.

clue.text: There's a place for bangers at an outdoor party?

definitions.text: There's a place for bangers at an outdoor party?

parts.words: There's a place for bangers at an outdoor party?
parts.note: bangers are British slang for sausages, cooked over the open flames at a camp gathering

explanation.walkthrough: 'bangers' suggests fireworks; in British slang they are sausages, grilled over open flames.
explanation.definitionFit: An open fire at a camp, around which people gather to cook and sing.

clue.text: I'm irate about how long programme goes on for

definitions.text: how long programme goes on for

indicators.note: about signals the letters of the angry phrase are moved around

explanation.surface: Someone fumes over the length of a TV show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges IMIRATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Broadcasting time allotted to a show, the minutes it is on screen.

clue.text: A cat for each and every Welsh woman?

parts.note: per means for each, as in miles per hour
Sian is a common Welsh girl's name

explanation.surface: Does every woman in Wales own a cat?
explanation.walkthrough: SIAN is a common Welsh girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-haired breed of domestic feline originally from Iran.

clue.text: It's good to get into seat with middle of stadium crowded

indicators.note: to get into says the letter for good is put inside the seat word

parts.note: a throne is a royal seat

indicators.note: the middle of a seven-letter word is its fourth letter, here from stadium

explanation.surface: Good seats are filled as the centre of the stadium is packed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get into' puts G inside THRONE, then 'middle of' adds the D at the centre of 'stadium'.
explanation.definitionFit: Filled by a large mass of people, a synonym of packed.

clue.text: Dear me — that's wrong — it must be done again!

indicators.note: wrong says these letters are out of their proper order and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: An exasperated boss sees a botched job and orders a redo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's wrong' rearranges DEARME.
explanation.definitionFit: Made once more, reconstructed, so redone.

clue.text: Concert performance's beginning on time, on the dot

parts.note: a prom is a promenade concert, as in the BBC Proms

indicators.note: beginning means the first letter of performance's

explanation.surface: A concert starts punctually.
explanation.walkthrough: A prom is a promenade concert, like London's BBC Proms summer season.
explanation.definitionFit: Punctual, arriving exactly on time.

clue.text: Using some venom, I'd get small insect

indicators.note: Using some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone plans to poison a tiny pest.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny two-winged fly that often swarms near water and bites.

clue.text: After end of pain I am fortunate to be most active

indicators.note: end of points to the final letter of pain

parts.note: contracted to I'm
blest, a variant of blessed, means fortunate

explanation.surface: Once the pain has gone, I feel lucky to be so sprightly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' just orders the pieces naturally: the N comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Superlative of agile or quick, so the most sprightly.

clue.text: Heather — primarily type that will catch fire easily?

indicators.note: primarily says the word for type is put first, ahead of the heather word

parts.note: kind means type, sort
ling is common heather

explanation.surface: Heather is mainly the sort of plant that burns readily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heather' looks like a woman's name but is the plant; 'primarily' puts the type word first.
explanation.definitionFit: Small sticks and twigs used to start a fire because they burn so readily.

clue.text: Time to squash doctrine producing consternation

indicators.note: to squash says the time word is pressed in around the doctrine word

parts.note: a day is a period of time
an ism is a doctrine or ideology

explanation.surface: A lack of time to crush a creed causes alarm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time' reads as a verb in the surface but is a period, a day; 'to squash' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Dismay is alarm and distress, a near synonym of consternation.

clue.text: One always rolls over then starts to look lively eventually — when it's given?

definitions.text: One always rolls over then starts to look lively eventually — when it's given?

indicators.note: rolls over says the pieces for one and always are turned and read backwards

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
ever means always

indicators.note: starts to means the first letters of the next three words

explanation.surface: A sleepy soldier turns over in bed and slowly comes round at the morning call.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rolls over' turns IEVER into REVEI; the first letters of 'look lively eventually' give LLE. The whole clue pictures a sleeping soldier woken by the bugle.
explanation.definitionFit: The bugle call that wakes soldiers in the morning, when sleepers roll over and stir.
